runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The first booster catch, on Flight 5 in October 2024, worked on the first try. On the latest flight, Flight 15, the new V3 booster aborted its catch and came down in the ocean, though the ship was caught by the tower for the first time. I couldn't save a notes page.

sections.heading: First booster catch (Flight 5)
points: Flight 5, October 13, 2024: first successful tower catch of a Super Heavy booster, achieved on the first attempt.
Booster was a first-generation vehicle; it returned to Starbase and was caught by the tower's chopstick arms.

sections.heading: Most recent attempt (Flight 15)
points: Flight 15 launched from Pad 2 at Starbase with a V3 booster and 33 Raptor 3 engines.
The booster's guidance system aborted the catch because it was not where it needed to be, and it made a controlled reentry into the ocean near Starbase instead.
It was the first catch attempt for a V3 booster; all four V3 boosters on Flights 12-15 have been lost.
Ship 42 was caught by the tower on this flight, the first ship catch.

sections.heading: Comparison
points: Flight 5 succeeded and began the catch era; Flight 15's booster did not get caught.
The most recent successful booster catches were on Flights 5, 7 and 8, all first-generation boosters.
Flight 15 is a bigger milestone for the ship than for the booster.

runs.goal: find out how the most recent Starship booster catch compares to the first booster catch
runs.detail: The first booster catch, on Flight 5 in October 2024, worked on the first try. The latest attempt, Flight 15 in November 2026, was called off for safety and the booster exploded offshore, though the ship was caught. I couldn't confirm the latest successful booster catch.

sections.heading: First booster catch (Flight 5, Oct 13, 2024)
points: Booster 12 flew on Flight 5 and was caught by the launch tower's chopstick arms at Starbase on the first try, a first for any rocket stage.
It was a manually commanded go for catch after SpaceX checked the booster and the tower.
It was a milestone toward full reusability of Starship.

sections.heading: Most recent booster catch attempt (Flight 15, Nov 2026)
points: Flight 15 was the first mission to try catching both booster and ship.

The booster catch was called off for safety reasons. The booster was diverted to an offshore splashdown and exploded. The cause was still under investigation, and a SpaceX statement said it was not a GNC issue.
The ship was caught by the tower on the following day, a first from orbit.

sections.heading: Comparison
points: Flight 5 was a clean booster catch on the first attempt. In Flight 15 the booster catch was aborted, while the ship catch succeeded.
Between them, other boosters were caught, such as Booster 14 on Flight 7, the second booster recovery.
I could not confirm details of the latest successful booster catch (possibly Flight 14), so this compares against the most recent attempt, Flight 15.

The most recent attempt, on Flight 15 in November 2026, was aborted for safety and the booster splashed down offshore and exploded, though the ship was caught the next day. I could not confirm the latest successful booster catch.

runs.goal: find out what the James Webb Space Telescope's mirror is made of and why
runs.detail: Webb's mirror segments are made of beryllium, coated with a very thin layer of gold. Beryllium is light and strong, and it keeps its shape in extreme cold. Gold reflects infrared light very well, which is what Webb observes.

sections.heading: Material
points: The 18 hexagonal primary mirror segments are made of beryllium, a light, strong metal.
Each segment has a very thin gold coating, applied by vacuum vapour deposition after polishing, with a thin protective glass layer on top.

sections.heading: Why beryllium
points: It is strong and light, which matters for a mirror 6.5 m wide that had to be launched.
It holds its shape at cryogenic temperatures, which suits Webb's very cold operating environment.

sections.heading: Why gold
points: Gold reflects infrared light well, and Webb is an infrared telescope.
Gold is relatively unreactive, so it does not tarnish easily.
